# Dimension 2 — Models available

Which models Codex exposes, how you pick one, how reasoning effort is
controlled, and whether a non-OpenAI backend is possible — compared against
Claude Code. Source details in [citations](../citations.md).

## Codex model IDs

Every ID appearing across the fetched OpenAI pages [7][28]:

| Model | ID | Status | Codex description (verbatim) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.6 Sol | `gpt-5.6-sol` (alias `gpt-5.6`) | current | "Flagship GPT-5.6 model with the strongest capability for complex coding, computer use, research, and cybersecurity." [7] |
| 5.6 Terra | `gpt-5.6-terra` | current | "Balanced GPT-5.6 model for everyday work, with performance competitive with GPT-5.5 at a lower cost." [7] |
| 5.6 Luna | `gpt-5.6-luna` | current | "Fast and affordable GPT-5.6 model that delivers strong capability at the lowest cost in the family." [7] |
| 5.3 Codex Spark | `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` | research preview, ChatGPT Pro only | "Text-only research preview model optimized for near-instant, real-time coding iteration." [7] |
| 5.5 | `gpt-5.5` | previous generation | "Previous-generation frontier model…" [7] |
| 5.4 | `gpt-5.4` | **retires from Codex 2026-08-31** | [7] |
| 5.4 Mini | `gpt-5.4-mini` | **retires from Codex 2026-08-31** | [7] |
| — | `gpt-5.2`, `gpt-5.3-codex` | already deprecated in Codex under ChatGPT sign-in | [7] |

> "GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 mini retire from Codex on August 31, 2026. If you sign in
> with ChatGPT, replace `gpt-5.4` with `gpt-5.6-terra` and `gpt-5.4-mini` with
> `gpt-5.6-luna` in saved configurations, custom agents, and scheduled tasks.
> The OpenAI API and Codex authenticated with your own API key aren't
> affected." [7]

That date is **ten days after this research was written**. Any Codex config
pinning `gpt-5.4` under ChatGPT sign-in has a hard expiry.

## Context windows

| Model | Context window | Max output | Knowledge cutoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gpt-5.6-sol` | `1.05M` | `128K tokens` | `Feb 16, 2026` |
| `gpt-5.6-terra` | `1.05M` | `128K tokens` | `Feb 16, 2026` |
| `gpt-5.6-luna` | `1.05M` | `128K tokens` | `Feb 16, 2026` |

All from the API models page [28], which writes the unit literally as `1.05M`
rather than a token count. **No Codex-surface page states a context window at
all** [7][8], and no fetched page gives one for `gpt-5.5`, `gpt-5.4`,
`gpt-5.4-mini` or `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`.

`model_context_window` exists as a `config.toml` key — "Context window tokens
available to the active model" — with **no documented default** [1]. The
`model_context_window = 128000` line in the advanced-config page is an
illustrative snippet value, not a model's window [3].

Claude Code side: "Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support
a 1 million token context window"; "On the Anthropic API, Sonnet 5 always runs
with the 1M context window. There is no 200K variant"; sessions auto-compact "at
about **967K tokens** by default", tunable with
`CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` [51]. Anthropic prices the full 1M window at
standard rates [58]; OpenAI charges a separate long-context rate roughly double
the short-context rate [30]. That is a real structural difference in what a
long session costs.

## Selecting a model

Codex [7]:

```
codex --model gpt-5.6            # or -m
codex exec -m gpt-5.6 "Review the current changes"
/model                           # interactive: switch model or reasoning effort
model = "gpt-5.6"                # config.toml
```

`model` is **not** on the project-scope ignore list, so a project
`.codex/config.toml` can set it [1]. "Currently, you can't change the default
model for Codex cloud chats" [7].

Claude Code offers a superset of routing surfaces: `/model <alias|name>`,
`claude --model`, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, the `model` settings field, and
`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` (v2.1.236+), in that precedence order [51]. Aliases:
`default`, `best`, `fable`, `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `sonnet[1m]`, `opus[1m]`,
`opusplan` [51].

**Structural asymmetry worth flagging.** Claude Code has an admin model
allowlist — `availableModels` plus `enforceAvailableModels`, matching a family
(`sonnet`), a version prefix, or a full ID, and applying to the session model,
subagent models, skill frontmatter and fast mode [51]. Codex's
`requirements.toml` has allowlists for approval policies, sandbox modes,
permission profiles and web-search modes, but **no model allowlist** [1]. Its
`[models.new_thread]` table "supplies managed defaults, not enforcement" [1].
This is an argument from that page's enumerated allowlist keys; a second source
would strengthen it.

Claude Code also supports fallback chains — `--fallback-model sonnet,haiku`,
capped at three models after dedup [51]. No Codex equivalent appears in the
fetched pages.

## Reasoning effort — three enumerations that do not agree

This is the single most confusing finding in the dimension. Three OpenAI
surfaces list different value sets, all fetched the same day:

| Surface | Values | Source |
|---|---|---|
| API `reasoning.effort` (prose) | "can include `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`" | [29] |
| API model cards (all three GPT-5.6) | `none low medium high xhigh max` — **no `minimal`** | [28] |
| Codex CLI interactive selector | Low, Medium (default), High, Extra high, **Max**, **Ultra** — six entries | [7] |
| Codex `config.toml` `model_reasoning_effort` | `minimal \| low \| medium \| high \| xhigh` — **no `max`, no `ultra`, no `none`** | [1] |

So the CLI picker offers two levels the config reference documents no key value
for. `plan_mode_reasoning_effort` separately accepts
`none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh` [1]. **This research could not
resolve how to persist Max or Ultra in config.**

Ultra is not merely "more thinking":

> "Ultra mode goes beyond a single-agent run. It uses subagents to accelerate
> complex work, making it useful for larger tasks that can be split across
> subagents." [7]

> "Max gives the selected model more time to reason about a single task." [7]

> "There is no exact mapping from GPT-5.5 reasoning efforts to GPT-5.6. Try a
> familiar task at a lower setting and adjust based on the result." [7]

A second, independent axis exists on GPT-5.6 in the Responses API:
`reasoning.mode` = `standard | pro`, where "Reasoning mode and reasoning effort
are independent" and pro "aggregates the model work performed to produce the
final answer and bills those tokens at the selected model's standard token
rates" [29]. Also `reasoning.context` = `auto | current_turn | all_turns`, with
GPT-5.6 defaulting to `all_turns` [29].

Claude Code's effort levels [51]:

| Models | Levels |
|---|---|
| Fable 5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7 | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` |
| Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max` |

"The default effort is `high` on every model that supports effort, except Opus
4.7, which defaults to `xhigh`" [51]. `max` is session-only unless set through
`CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`; `effortLevel` in settings accepts only
`low | medium | high | xhigh` [51]. Note Anthropic's own warning: "The effort
scale is calibrated per model, so the same level name does not represent the
same underlying value across models" [51] — which applies across vendors at
least as strongly.

Claude Code's `ultracode` is the closest analogue to Codex's Ultra: "it sends
`xhigh` to the model and additionally has Claude orchestrate dynamic workflows
for substantive tasks", session-only [51]. Both vendors now ship a top setting
that changes orchestration, not just token budget.

## Non-OpenAI and open-weight backends

Codex documents this explicitly, with worked examples [3]:

```toml
model = "gpt-5.6-terra"
model_provider = "proxy"

[model_providers.proxy]
name = "OpenAI using LLM proxy"
base_url = "http://proxy.example.com"
env_key = "OPENAI_API_KEY"

[model_providers.local_ollama]
name = "Ollama"
base_url = "http://localhost:11434/v1"

[model_providers.mistral]
name = "Mistral"
base_url = "https://api.mistral.ai/v1"
env_key = "MISTRAL_API_KEY"
```

Constraints [1][3]:

- Built-in provider IDs `openai`, `ollama`, `lmstudio` are **reserved** and
  cannot be overridden. To repoint the built-in OpenAI provider, use
  `openai_base_url` instead of defining `[model_providers.openai]`.
- `wire_api` — "`responses` is the only supported value, and it is the default
  when omitted" [1]. **But** the models page says "You can also point Codex at
  any model and provider that supports either the Chat Completions or Responses
  APIs" while adding "Support for the Chat Completions API is deprecated and
  will be removed in future releases" [7]. **These two statements conflict as
  of the same fetch date and this research does not resolve them.**
- Command-backed auth exists: `[model_providers.<id>.auth]` with `command`,
  `args`, `refresh_interval_ms` (default 300000), `timeout_ms` (default 5000);
  must not be combined with `env_key` or `requires_openai_auth` [1][3].
- A built-in `amazon-bedrock` provider exists, taking only nested
  `aws.profile` / `aws.region` overrides [1][3].
- Local open-weight mode: `codex --oss`, with `--local-provider lmstudio|ollama`
  or a default `oss_provider`. "If neither is set, the interactive CLI prompts
  you to choose; `codex exec` exits with an error." [3]

**Critical for a sandbox that uploads config:** `model_provider`,
`model_providers` and `openai_base_url` are all on the ten-key project-scope
ignore list [1]. They must be in the user-level `~/.codex/config.toml`.

Claude Code's documented extensibility is different in kind. The model-config
page describes *routing* — `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` ("changes where requests are
sent, not which model answers them"), gateway model discovery,
`ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION`, `modelOverrides` mapping Anthropic IDs to
Bedrock ARNs or Foundry deployment names [51]. **Nothing on that page describes
configuring a non-Anthropic model.** That is a difference in what the two
vendors *document*, not a proven difference in what the binaries permit.

## Benchmarks — read OpenAI's own retraction first

Before comparing any SWE-bench number between these tools, note that OpenAI
published a paper on **2026-02-23** telling you not to [31]:

> "SWE-bench Verified is increasingly contaminated. We recommend SWE-bench
> Pro." [31]

> "This means that improvements on SWE-bench Verified no longer reflect
> meaningful improvements in models' real-world software development abilities.
> Instead, they increasingly reflect how much the model was exposed to the
> benchmark at training time. This is why we have stopped reporting SWE-bench
> Verified scores, and we recommend that other model developers do so too." [31]

The evidence, with its exact scope:

- State of the art moved "from 74.9% to 80.9% in the last 6 months" — **OpenAI's
  prose, hyperlinked to llm-stats.com, not OpenAI's own measurement** [31].
- OpenAI audited **138 of the 500** problems (27.6%) that OpenAI o3 failed to
  solve consistently across 64 runs, each reviewed by "at least six experienced
  software engineers". **59.4% of those 138** had material defects: 35.5% narrow
  test cases, 18.8% wide test cases, 5.1% miscellaneous [31]. That percentage
  applies to the hard subset, not to all 500 — OpenAI's own phrasing is "at
  least 59.4% of the audited problems".
- "all frontier models we tested were able to reproduce the original,
  human-written bug fix used as the ground-truth reference… indicating that all
  of them have seen at least some of the problems and solutions during
  training" [31]. Verbatim-recall examples are given for GPT-5.2, Claude Opus
  4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash Preview [31].
- The contamination probe deliberately used non-reasoning chat models, and
  OpenAI concedes "there is likely a non-trivial capability gap between them"
  [31].
- Even the recommended replacement is hedged: "SWE-bench Pro is not perfect, but
  empirically seems to suffer less from contamination issues" [31].

Note also that OpenAI authored SWE-bench Verified and is the party recommending
its retirement in favour of a benchmark on which it reports its own results.

**This research found no head-to-head SWE-bench Pro table comparing current
Codex models against current Claude models.** Any such comparison would have to
be built from sources not in this citation pool.

## Gaps and limitations

1. **No context window is published for `gpt-5.5`, `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.4-mini` or
   `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`.** Only the three GPT-5.6 models are documented, at
   `1.05M` [28].
2. **No config value for Max or Ultra reasoning effort is documented** [1] even
   though the CLI picker offers both [7].
3. **`wire_api` conflict unresolved** — Chat Completions is simultaneously
   described as supported-but-deprecated [7] and as not an accepted value [1].
4. The models page's per-model surface-availability matrix (CLI vs desktop vs
   cloud) did not survive extraction, so which surfaces expose
   `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` and `gpt-5.5` is unestablished [7].
5. Whether a custom `model_providers` entry works under ChatGPT sign-in or
   requires API-key auth is not addressed by any fetched page.
6. The default model when `config.toml` sets none is described only as "a
   recommended model" [7]; the `gpt-5.6-sol medium` figure comes from a
   marketing mockup [8].
7. The Codex-model-vs-Claude-model capability comparison this dimension was
   meant to support **cannot be made from cited evidence**. The only benchmark
   source in the pool is OpenAI's own argument that the standard benchmark is
   invalid [31].
